explainers.title: Hello again, and welcome to Analysis
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. In Unit 1 you built your very first thinking skill, Research. You learned to choose an issue, ask good questions, gather information from people and places, and record what you found in a tidy way. That was a wonderful start. Now you are ready to build the next skill on top of it.

Remember that this subject grows six thinking skills, and each one helps the others:

This whole unit is about the second skill: Analysis. Research helped you find out what is happening. Analysis asks the deeper questions: why is it happening, who sees it differently, and what does it lead to? Once you have gathered good information, analysis is how you make sense of it. And it is something you already do a little every day, even if you have never called it that.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way, which means three kinds of support work together:

Analysis grows fastest through talking, because it is all about seeing an issue from more than one side. In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss as a class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So treat every 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box as a real conversation: say your idea, then ask the tutor to argue the other side, to test whether your thinking holds up.

Just as in Unit 1, your analysis skills will grow in three stages this year, like a young tree growing taller: you will start each skill, then develop it, and finally get better at it. Do not worry if something feels tricky at first. Starting is meant to feel like a first try.
bullets: You, at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea, such as telling a fact from an opinion, or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a friendly study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It will discuss your ideas, gently challenge your thinking, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best analysis, ask the questions that matter most, and hear how other learners see the same issue.

explainers.title: Meet Nadir, our analyst for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each idea clear, we will follow one Year 6 learner all the way through the unit. His name is Nadir, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. Now it is his turn to analyse an issue that is all around him.

Nadir has started to notice how much energy it takes to power an ordinary day. At school, a diesel generator hums in the yard; it runs the lights and fans, but it is noisy and puffs out grey smoke. At home, his family cooks over charcoal, and in the evening they light a lamp so he can do his homework, while some neighbours have fitted a small solar panel on the roof. Nadir starts to ask himself: how do we power our lives, what does it cost us in money, health and the land around us, and could clean energy like solar help?

That question becomes Nadir's project for this unit. Notice that he is no longer only finding out about energy, as he would in Research; he is taking the issue apart, looking for causes, consequences, and the many perspectives around him. As you meet each analysis skill, you will see what Nadir does with it, and do the very same thing with an issue that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
Just like in Research, this unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge: a real issue that matters where you live and also connects to the wider world. You will keep returning to it, lesson after lesson, and each new analysis skill adds another layer to it.

You have a choice. You may keep the same Challenge topic you researched in Unit 1 and now analyse it more deeply, which is a great option because you already have information about it. Or you may choose a new issue if something else has caught your attention. Here are some issues that are very real in the Horn of Africa and full of different perspectives:

The best issue for Analysis is one where people honestly see things differently. If everyone already agrees, there is little to analyse, so look for a topic where a herder, a shopkeeper, a parent and a student might each say something different.
bullets: How our school and our homes use energy, and what it costs us
Charcoal and firewood for cooking, and the cutting of trees
Solar power for light and for charging phones
Clean air, and the fumes from generators and traffic near school
Healthy and unhealthy snacks at school
The livestock and other goods our region sells to the rest of the world
Following the news, and staying safe online
Clean water for every family in the dry season

explainers.title: So what is analysis?
explainers.body:
The word analysis means breaking something into its parts so you can understand it better. When you analyse an issue, you stop treating it as one big lump and start asking careful questions about the pieces inside it: What exactly is the problem? Why is it happening? What does it lead to? Who is affected, and how do they see it? A useful way to remember it is this: research gathers the pieces, and analysis works out how the pieces fit together.

Good analysis uses several kinds of thinking, and this unit will teach you each one:

That may look long, but almost every part answers one of three simple questions: What is going on? Why? And so what? Keep those three questions in mind and analysis will feel natural.
bullets: Seeing different perspectives, at three sizes: personal, local or national, and global.
Telling a fact from an opinion.
Explaining the causes of a local issue and its consequences for people.
Finding patterns in data, such as a bar chart or table, and saying what they mean.
Naming the stakeholders, and who is for or against.
Weighing the arguments for and against different solutions.
Writing a justification for a solution, and judging how good one is.
Noticing persuasive words that show a strong feeling.
Working out the impacts of a solution on different groups.
Telling what we know for sure from what we can reasonably conclude, and linking local and global issues.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Perspectives, at three sizes
explainers.body:
The first big idea in Analysis is the perspective: a way of looking at an issue, shaped by who a person is, where they live, and what they care about. On almost any issue, people honestly think differently, and each person's view is based on their own evidence and reasoning. A good analyst does not decide who is right straight away; first they try to see the issue through each person's eyes.

The closest perspective is your own, called a personal perspective. But perspectives also come at bigger sizes. It helps to sort them into three:

Strong analysis moves between these three sizes instead of getting stuck at just one. A learner who only sees the personal size misses the bigger picture, while one who only talks about the global forgets the real people next door.
bullets: A personal perspective is how the issue looks to you and your own family, up close.
A local or national perspective is the point of view of a place or a whole country.
A global perspective is about how the issue affects many countries, or the whole planet.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Telling a fact from an opinion
explainers.body:
When you analyse what people say and write, you must sort two very different things: facts and opinions. Mixing them up is one of the easiest mistakes to make, and one of the most important to avoid.

Both matter in analysis. Facts give you solid ground; opinions tell you how people feel and what they value, which is what perspectives are made of. The skill is not to throw opinions away, but to know which is which, so you never treat a strong opinion as if it were a proven fact.
bullets: A fact is something that can be checked and shown to be true, such as a count, a measurement or a date.
An opinion is what someone thinks, feels or believes. It cannot simply be looked up, and other people may honestly disagree.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Causes and consequences
explainers.body:
At the centre of analysis is a simple pair of questions: why did this happen, and what does it lead to? The answers are the causes and the consequences.

Most issues have more than one cause and more than one consequence, and one consequence can become the cause of the next problem, like dominoes falling. Seeing that chain clearly is a big part of analysis, because it shows both why a problem exists and what harm it does, which is what you need before you can suggest a helpful change.
bullets: A cause is a reason why an issue or a situation happens.
A consequence is a result or an effect that follows from it.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Finding patterns in data
explainers.body:
Not all evidence is words. Some of the strongest evidence is data: numbers, counts and measurements, often shown in a bar chart or a table. A good analyst can read a chart and describe the pattern in it. A pattern is something the data does again and again, such as one bar being tallest, or numbers rising or falling in order.

When you meet a chart, read it in a calm order: first the title (what is it about?), then the labels (what is being counted?), then the bars or numbers themselves (which is biggest, which is smallest?). Comparing two groups side by side often reveals the most, because you can spot a similarity and a difference at the same time.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Stakeholders, and who is for or against
explainers.body: Every issue has people who care about it, and the word for them is stakeholders. A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue, because it affects them or they can affect it. Some are in favour and some are against; some have a lot of influence over what happens, and some are simply affected by it. Listing the stakeholders is one of the best ways to make sure you have not missed an important perspective. To find their views, name each one, then ask how they would finish the sentence: the most important thing about this issue is...

explainers.title: Skill 6: Arguments for and against solutions
explainers.body:
Once you understand an issue, you begin to think about solutions: the actions people could take to make it better. Most issues have several possible solutions, each with arguments in favour and arguments against. A careful analyst does not fall in love with the first idea, but weighs the good and the bad points of each one before choosing.

Imagine a class analysing the dust and fumes at a busy school gate in Mogadishu, where cars idle and honk at drop-off time. They list several possible actions:
bullets: A 'No-Stopping' zone, so cars cannot idle right at the entrance.
Bright awareness posters, made by students, about clean air.
A line of hardy trees and shrubs along the fence to catch dust and fumes.
A whole-school assembly, with parents invited, about traffic and health.
A reward scheme, giving points to children who walk, cycle or share a ride.
Asking the town for a proper crossing and a traffic officer at busy times.

explainers.title: Skill 7: Justifying a solution, and judging a justification
explainers.body: When you choose a solution, you must be able to explain why. That explanation is called a justification: the set of reasons you give for the action you have chosen. A strong justification does not just say 'I like this idea'; it gives reasons, points to research, names the benefits, and is honest about the limitations.
bullets: Does it give a global reason as well as a local one, so it connects to the bigger picture?
Does it consider different local perspectives, not just the writer's own?
Does it use real research and evidence, not only feelings?
Is it honest about both the strengths and the weaknesses of the solution?

explainers.title: Skill 8: Persuasive words and strength of feeling
explainers.body:
When people care about an issue, the words they choose often show how strongly they feel. Some words are calm and neutral, while others are chosen to make you feel something and to persuade you. Spotting these words helps you understand a perspective, and later it helps you write in a way that moves people, too.

One helpful trick is to place different views on a line, or a spectrum, from strongly against to strongly in favour:
bullets: Strongly against, then somewhat against, then neutral, then somewhat in favour, then strongly in favour.
The strongest views usually use the strongest words.

explainers.title: Skill 9: The impacts of a solution on different groups
explainers.body:
Before you cheer for a solution, a careful analyst asks one more question: how would it affect different groups of people? The effects of a solution are called its impacts, and they are rarely the same for everyone. Thinking about impacts stops you from suggesting an action that is unfair to someone you forgot.

A neat way to do this is an impacts table. You write your solution at the top, then list the groups down the side, and note how each one is affected.

explainers.title: Skill 10: What we know for sure, and what we can reasonably conclude
explainers.body: When you have gathered data, there are two kinds of statement you can make about it, and a good analyst never muddles them. Some things the data proves, so you know them for sure. Other things the data hints at, so you can reasonably conclude them, but you cannot be certain. Saying more than your data proves is called over-claiming, and it makes your work weaker.

explainers.title: Skill 11: Connections between local and global issues
explainers.body: The last analysis skill is a beautiful one: seeing how a local issue on your own street connects to a global issue that touches the whole world. Once you can trace this connection, small choices at home stop feeling small, because you can see how they join up with the wider world.

explainers.title: Staying fair when you analyse
explainers.body:
Analysis gives you the power to take an issue apart, so it also asks you to be fair. The heart of Global Perspectives is seeing an issue from many sides evenly, before you decide. A fair analyst listens to perspectives they disagree with just as carefully as ones they like.

People's perspectives are shaped by where they live, their work, their age, their family, and their beliefs. Noticing this helps you understand a viewpoint instead of just brushing it aside.

explainers.title: How analysis links to the other five skills
explainers.body:
Analysis sits in the middle of the six skills and connects to every one of them, taking what research gives you and preparing the way for what follows.

So the thinking you practise here is never wasted. Analysis is the bridge between simply knowing about an issue and being able to judge it, discuss it, and act on it wisely.
bullets: Research feeds analysis: you cannot break an issue into causes and perspectives until you have gathered good information.
Evaluation builds on analysis: once you can see the different views, evaluation helps you judge which arguments are actually strongest.
Reflection grows every time you notice how your analysis changed your mind about an issue.
Collaboration improves when you can understand other people's perspectives instead of only your own.
Communication becomes clearer and fairer when it rests on careful analysis rather than a first reaction.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the analysis cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every analysis skill in this unit. Here is how they fit into one clear cycle you can use for any issue:
bullets: See the different perspectives, at three sizes: personal, local or national, and global.
Sort the facts from the opinions.
Map the causes and consequences, following the chain.
Find the patterns in any data, and name the stakeholders who are for or against.
Weigh the arguments for and against each solution.
Justify your chosen solution, and check its impacts on different groups.
Say what you know for sure, what you can reasonably conclude, and how the local links to the global.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Evaluation. Once you can analyse an issue, evaluation teaches you to weigh those arguments and pieces of evidence and judge how strong each one really is. Strong analysis now will make strong evaluation much easier later. Well done for taking your thinking to a new level in Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is like a bus, and the skill is where the bus takes you.
We will use real issues such as energy, clean air, snacks and trade, but the point is not to become an expert on charcoal or buses.
The point is to become a clear thinker who can take almost any issue apart, see it from many sides, and reach a fair conclusion.

bigIdeas.title: A fairness note for Global Perspectives
lines: People often see the same issue in very different ways, and that is normal.
One family lights a generator so the children can study in the evening. A neighbour dislikes the noise and the fumes. A shopkeeper is glad, because people pay to charge their phones.
A good analyst listens to all these perspectives fairly, instead of only their own. Seeing an issue from many sides is the very heart of Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: A quick test for a fact or an opinion
lines: Ask: can this be checked or counted? If yes, it is probably a fact.
Ask: could sensible people disagree with it? If yes, it is probably an opinion.
Feeling words like best, worst, terrible or wonderful often signal an opinion.
When someone gives an opinion, a good analyst asks: what fact or evidence backs this up?

bigIdeas.title: Signal words that point to causes and consequences
lines: Words that point to a cause: because, since, due to, the reason is, caused by.
Words that point to a consequence: so, therefore, as a result, this means that, this leads to.
When you read a source, underline these words. They point straight to the reasons and the effects.

bigIdeas.title: Even one group can hold different perspectives
lines: Stakeholders in the same group often share a perspective, but not always.
Two herders might disagree: one wants to sell more animals abroad, while another worries the land cannot feed so many.
So when you name a group, still ask whether everyone inside it would truly say the same thing.

bigIdeas.title: Answering an objection makes a justification stronger
lines: After Nadir explained his plan, Leila raised a fair objection: solar panels cost a lot to buy, and the school may not have the money.
A weak analyst ignores an objection. A strong one answers it.
Nadir replied: the school could start with just a few panels, raise funds at a community day, or ask for help, and still cut the generator's fumes and bills over time.
By meeting the objection, Nadir made his justification more honest and more convincing.

bigIdeas.title: Two careful sentence starters
lines: Use 'We know for sure that...' only when your data clearly proves it.
Use 'We can reasonably conclude that...' when your data points that way but does not fully prove it.
If you cannot back a statement with your data at all, do not make it yet.

bigIdeas.title: Different lives, different perspectives
lines: Imagine a school choosing the day for a big sports afternoon during a time of fasting.
A family that fasts for Ramadan and a family that fasts during Lent might each have a clear view on the timing.
Neither view is simply right or wrong; each comes from that family's way of life.
A fair analyst hears both evenly and looks for a plan that respects everyone.

bigIdeas.title: Watch out for bias
lines: Bias is when a source or a person leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
A view is not automatically wrong because it takes a side, but you should notice the side it takes.
Balance a strong view from one group by finding an equally strong view from another.
Being fair does not mean having no opinion. It means forming your opinion only after hearing many sides.

bigIdeas.title: The three questions of analysis
lines: Whenever you feel stuck, come back to these three simple questions.
What is going on? Name the issue clearly.
Why? Find the causes and the different perspectives.
So what? Follow the consequences and reach a fair conclusion.
Every tool in this file helps you answer one of these three questions.

bigIdeas.title: Remember
lines: Facts give you solid ground; opinions tell you how people feel.
You need both, but you must always know which is which.
A strong perspective is an opinion backed by evidence.

bigIdeas.title: Signal words to look for
lines: Cause words: because, since, due to, the reason is, caused by.
Consequence words: so, therefore, as a result, this means that, this leads to.
Underline these in any source; they point straight to causes and effects.

bigIdeas.title: Judging how good a justification is
lines: Does it give a global reason as well as a local one?
Does it consider different local perspectives, not just the writer's own?
Does it use real research and evidence, not only feelings?
Is it honest about both the strengths and the weaknesses?

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Choose one real issue to analyse across this whole unit. This is your Challenge.
You may keep the topic you researched in Unit 1, or pick a new issue where people see things differently.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you genuinely care about.

bigIdeas.title: The survey result
lines: Nadir's group asked 150 people at school which action they most wanted for cleaner air at the gate.
The reward scheme for walking got 48 votes, the most of any action.
The line of trees got 34 votes. The other four actions each got fewer than 25.
For each statement, write 'know for sure', 'reasonably conclude', or 'cannot say from this data', and give a short reason.

models.title: Analysis happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine the light in your home keeps going out just as you sit down to study.
Research would ask: is it only our house, or the whole street?
Analysis goes further. It asks why: perhaps the generator is off to save fuel, or everyone is charging phones at once, or the battery is old.
It asks about consequences and perspectives too: your homework is late, and while you worry about that, your parent worries about the cost of fuel.
Working all of that out, not just noticing the dark room, is analysis. You already do it.

models.title: Nadir sorts three perspectives on energy
lines: Personal: since we got a small solar lamp, I can do my homework at night without the smoky kerosene lamp. This is one person's own experience.
Local or national: our country spends a lot of money bringing in fuel from abroad, money that could build schools and clinics.
Global: burning charcoal, coal and fuel puts gases into the air that warm the whole planet.
It is one issue, energy, seen at three sizes. Each size adds something the others miss.

models.title: Sana sorts facts from opinions about school snacks
lines: Sana is analysing the snacks children buy from the little shop by the school gate.
Fact: eating a lot of sugar can lead to tooth decay. This is known and can be checked.
Fact: many crisp and sweet packets are made of plastic that is hard to recycle. This can be checked too.
Opinion: sweets taste far nicer than fruit. This is a feeling, and some people would disagree.
Opinion: the shop should not be allowed to sell sweets to children. This is a belief about what ought to happen, not a proven fact.
Sana keeps all four, but she labels each one, so she never confuses how people feel with what is true.

models.title: Karim maps the causes and consequences of charcoal
lines: Karim is analysing why so many families in his neighbourhood cook over charcoal.
Causes: charcoal is cheap to buy in small amounts, the stoves are simple, and it is what families have always used.
Consequences: as a result, many trees are cut down to make charcoal, the smoke is unhealthy to breathe indoors, and as trees vanish the land dries out.
Notice the chain: cutting trees for charcoal leads to barer land, which leads to worse dust and drought, which then makes life harder for everyone.

models.title: Nadia compares how children and adults follow the news
lines: Nadia is analysing how people get their news. She looks at two bar charts side by side: one for adults, one for children.
For adults, the tallest bars are television and radio, and quite a few read a newspaper.
For children, the tallest bars are family and friends, and online, while very few read a newspaper.
A similarity: both children and adults use television a lot.
A difference: children lean on family, friends and online, while adults use radio and newspapers more. So news reaches children in a very different way.

Before you study a chart closely, it is a good habit to make a prediction: a smart guess about what the data will show, then check the chart against it. Whether you were right or wrong, comparing your guess with the real pattern is analysis in action.

models.title: Idris lists the stakeholders in the livestock trade
lines: The Horn of Africa sells millions of sheep and goats across the sea each year, especially around Hajj and Eid. Idris lists who has a stake in this trade.
A herder near Burao: I walk my animals far to find water and grass, and the traders pay me little, but selling to the ships is still my main income.
A family in the Gulf buying meat for Eid: we are glad we can buy healthy animals from the Horn of Africa when we need a great many.
An environmental campaigner: shipping so many animals across the sea burns fuel, and too many animals on dry land can strip it bare.
A trader at Berbera port: this trade brings money into the whole country, but prices are tight, so I cannot pay the herders much more.
A farmer in the Gulf who raises a few animals: the imported ones are cheaper than mine, so I struggle to sell what I raise.

models.title: Rami weighs one solution: the reward scheme
lines: In favour: it is cheerful and fun, it could cut the number of cars, and it costs very little.
Against: some children live too far to walk, prizes cost something, and the effect might fade once the prizes stop.
Rami does the same for each of the six actions, listing points on both sides.
Only after weighing them all does he decide which action he thinks is strongest, and why.
Weighing arguments does not mean you must stay silent. It means you earn the right to your opinion by looking fairly at both sides first, which is what makes your final choice convincing.

models.title: Nadir justifies solar panels for the school
lines: Nadir's chosen solution: put solar panels on the school roof, and switch off the diesel generator during the day.
His reasons and research: generator smoke can harm breathing; the sun shines strongly here for most of the year; after the first cost, solar power is cheap to run.
The benefits: cleaner air in the classrooms, quieter lessons, and lower fuel bills over time.
He is honest about a limitation, too: solar panels cost a lot to buy at the start.
Just as important as writing a justification is being able to judge one, your own or someone else's. To weigh how good a justification is, ask four questions:

models.title: Amara notices the strength of feeling about the livestock trade
lines: One speaker says: this trade is the proud backbone of our economy, and we must protect it. The words proud, backbone and must show a strong feeling in favour.
Another says: it is cruel to pack so many animals onto ships, and it is ruining our dry land. The words cruel and ruining show a strong feeling against.
A third says calmly: the trade has some good points and some bad points. That is a neutral view, with gentle words.
Amara can now place each speaker on the spectrum, just from the strength of their words.

Noticing persuasive words does not mean the strong speakers are wrong. It simply means you can tell the difference between a calm fact and a feeling dressed in powerful words, so nobody can sweep you along without evidence.

models.title: Nadir works out the impacts of solar panels at school
lines: Younger children: cleaner air to play in, and lessons no longer stop when the noisy generator coughs.
Older children: they can charge lights and tablets for evening study, and they learn about clean energy.
Parents: lower fuel bills for the school over time, though some worry about the high cost of buying the panels.
School staff: quieter classrooms, but someone must learn to look after the panels.
The wider community: a visible example that might encourage others to try solar, although the diesel seller loses some business.
Notice that the impacts are not all good. Naming the losers as well as the winners is what makes the analysis fair.

models.title: Nadir's group survey which clean-air action people want
lines: Nadir's group asked 150 people at school which action they most wanted for cleaner air at the gate.
The reward scheme for walking got the most votes, with 48. The line of trees came next, with 34. The others got fewer.
We know for sure that the reward scheme was the most popular choice, because the votes clearly show it.
We can reasonably conclude that many children like the idea of earning a reward, which is a fair guess from the votes.
But we cannot be sure the reward would actually cut the traffic. The survey never measured that, so claiming it would be over-claiming.

models.title: Nadir connects his street to the whole planet
lines: Local: on Nadir's street, families burn charcoal to cook and run generators for light, and the school gate fills with fumes.
Global: all around the world, burning fuel and cutting trees add gases to the air that warm the planet and change the weather.
The circle closes: a warmer planet can bring worse droughts and dust back to the Horn of Africa, which makes daily life harder at home.
So a local choice, such as switching to a solar lamp, is also a small part of a global answer. Nadir finds that idea powerful.

The livestock trade shows the same connection from another angle: a herder's local work is tied to the demand for meat in faraway countries. Local and global are not two separate worlds; they are two ends of the same thread, and analysis is how you follow it.

models.title: Nadir's whole journey, from a smoky generator to a plan
lines: Skill 1: he saw the energy issue at three sizes, from his own lamp to the whole planet.
Skills 2 and 3: he sorted facts from opinions, and mapped the causes and consequences of charcoal and generators.
Skills 4 and 5: he read the data and listed every stakeholder, from families to the diesel seller.
Skills 6 and 7: he weighed the arguments for each solution, then justified solar panels and answered an objection.
Skills 8 and 9: he noticed the strong words people used, and worked out the impacts of solar on every group.
Skills 10 and 11: he said only what his survey proved, and connected his street's fumes to a global problem.

By following this cycle, Nadir turned a noisy, smoky problem into clear thinking and a fair plan. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge issue, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model: fact or opinion
lines: Statement: the clinic treated more coughs during the dusty months. This is a fact, because it is a record that can be checked.
Statement: dust is the worst problem our town has. This is an opinion, because others might name a different problem.
A fact that could test that opinion: how many people the clinic treats for dust compared with other illnesses.

toolkit.title: The analysis cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your issue, good analysis follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel lost.
items: See the perspectives: at three sizes, personal, local or national, and global.
Sort fact from opinion: know which is which.
Map causes and consequences: ask why it happens and what it leads to.
Find patterns and stakeholders: read the data and list who is for and against.
Weigh the arguments: for and against each solution.
Justify and check impacts: give your reasons, and see who gains and who loses.
Conclude carefully: say what you know for sure, and link the local to the global.

toolkit.title: The Analysis skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it better. Instead of treating a problem as one big lump, you ask careful questions about the pieces inside it: What exactly is the issue? Why is it happening (causes)? What does it lead to (consequences)? Who is affected, and how do they see it (perspectives)? Then you bring the pieces back together into a fair conclusion.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always look for more than one perspective, because every issue looks different depending on who is standing where. Second, always ask for the evidence behind a view, so you never mistake a strong opinion for a proven fact. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 6 Analysis learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your analysis skills grow in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: A guide to perspectives at three sizes
toolkit.intro: Use all three sizes so you do not think too narrowly. Ask: whose point of view is this, and how far does it reach?

rows: How the issue looks to me and my own family, up close.
Our solar lamp lets me study without smoke.
The view of a place or a whole country.
Our country spends a lot on fuel from abroad.
How the issue affects many countries or the whole planet.
Burning fuel warms the whole world.

toolkit.title: A cause, consequence and solution map
toolkit.intro: For any issue, fill in why it happens, what it leads to, and what could help. Watch for a consequence that becomes the cause of a new problem.

rows: Chain (a consequence that causes a new problem)

toolkit.title: A guide to reading a chart or table for patterns
toolkit.intro:
Read a chart in this order so it cannot fool you.

A bar chart shows amounts as bars of different heights, so the biggest and smallest stand out. Putting two charts or two columns side by side lets you spot a similarity and a difference at the same time. Before you look closely, make a prediction, then check it against the real pattern.
items: Read the title: what is the chart about?
Read the labels: what is being counted, and in what units?
Look at the bars or numbers: which is biggest, which is smallest?
Name the pattern: is one bar tallest, or do the numbers rise or fall in order?
Ask why: what might have caused the pattern?

toolkit.title: A stakeholder for-and-against spectrum
toolkit.intro:
List everyone with an interest in your issue, then place each one on a line from against to in favour. It reveals the full range of perspectives.

Remember two things: some stakeholders have a lot of influence while others are simply affected, and even people in the same group can hold different perspectives.

rows: Sees good and bad points evenly.
Sees it as very important and good.

toolkit.title: A frame for writing a justification
toolkit.intro: A justification is the set of reasons for the solution you choose. Fill in this frame to build a strong one.

rows: Why it would help, with facts or evidence.
The good things it would bring, and for whom.
My fair judgement, having weighed both sides.

toolkit.title: Know for sure, or reasonably conclude?
toolkit.intro:
When you draw conclusions from data, say only what the data allows. Sort each statement into one of these three.

Saying more than your data proves is called over-claiming, and it makes your analysis weaker. When in doubt, choose the more careful statement.

rows: The reward scheme got the most votes (48 of 150).
The data hints at it, but does not fully prove it.
Many children like the idea of a reward.
We cannot say from this data ...
The data does not tell us either way.
The reward scheme would cut the traffic.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for analysis
toolkit.intro: Use these to write clear analysis. Mix and match them as you need.

toolkit.title: For perspectives and causes:
items: From a personal, local or global point of view, ...
One group sees this as ... while another sees it as ...
This happens because ... , which leads to ...
As a result of this, ...

toolkit.title: For solutions and justifications:
items: One argument in favour is ... , but one argument against is ...
I would choose this solution because ...
One benefit is ... , and one honest limitation is ...
This solution would affect ... by ...

toolkit.title: For careful conclusions:
items: We know for sure that ...
We can reasonably conclude that ...
This local issue connects to the global issue of ...
Having weighed all sides, I think that ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Is it a fact or an opinion?
checklists.intro: Ask these questions about any statement before you rely on it.
items: Can it be checked or counted? If yes, it is probably a fact.
Could sensible people disagree with it? If yes, it is probably an opinion.
Does it use feeling words like best, worst, terrible or wonderful? Those often signal an opinion.
If it is an opinion, ask: what fact or evidence supports it?

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'analysis' mean?
practice.answer: Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it, by asking why it happens, what it leads to, and how different people see it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: What is a perspective?
practice.answer: A perspective is a way of looking at an issue, a point of view shaped by who someone is and where they live.

practice.prompt: Name the three sizes of perspective.
practice.answer: Personal; local or national; and global.

practice.prompt: True or false: 'Sweets taste nicer than fruit' is a fact.
practice.answer: False. It is an opinion, because others might disagree; it cannot be checked.

practice.prompt: A ______ is the reason why something happens; a ______ is the result of it happening.
practice.answer: A cause is the reason why something happens; a consequence is the result.

practice.prompt: Give one signal word that points to a cause, and one that points to a consequence.
practice.answer: Cause word: any of because, since, due to, the reason is. Consequence word: any of so, therefore, as a result, this leads to.

practice.prompt: What is a stakeholder?
practice.answer: A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue, because it affects them or they can affect it.

practice.prompt: When you read a chart, what does the word 'pattern' mean?
practice.answer: A pattern is something the data does again and again, such as one bar being tallest, or numbers rising or falling in order.

practice.prompt: A justification is the set of ______ you give for the solution you choose.
practice.answer: Reasons.

practice.prompt: Name two of the four questions you ask to judge how good a justification is.
practice.answer: Any two of: does it give a global reason as well as a local one? does it consider different local perspectives? does it use research? is it honest about strengths and weaknesses?

practice.prompt: Words like 'cruel', 'proud' and 'must' often show the ______ of feeling in a view.
practice.answer: Strength.

practice.prompt: The effects of a solution on different groups of people are called its ______.
practice.answer: Impacts.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between 'we know for sure' and 'we can reasonably conclude'?
practice.answer: We know for sure what the data clearly proves; we can reasonably conclude what the data hints at but does not fully prove.

practice.prompt: Saying more than your data proves is called ______.
practice.answer: Over-claiming.

practice.prompt: Give one example of how a local issue can be connected to a global issue.
practice.answer: Any sensible example, such as: burning charcoal locally adds to global warming, which can bring worse droughts back home.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Karim says the trees are being cut down because charcoal is cheap, so the land is turning to dust. Which part is a cause, and which is a consequence?
practice.answer: Cause: charcoal is cheap, so trees are cut down. Consequence: the land turns to dust.

practice.prompt: A herder is glad of the livestock trade, while a campaigner says it harms the land. What is the issue, and what are the two perspectives?
practice.answer: The issue is the livestock trade. The two perspectives are the herder's (it is my living) and the campaigner's (it harms the land).

practice.prompt: Sana read: 'The clinic treated more coughs during the dusty months.' Is this a fact or an opinion, and how could she check it?
practice.answer: It is a fact, because it is a record that can be checked. Sana could ask the clinic for its records or compare months.

practice.prompt: Nadir's survey shows the reward scheme got the most votes. Write one thing he knows for sure, and one he can only reasonably conclude.
practice.answer: Knows for sure: the reward scheme got the most votes. Reasonably concludes: many children like the idea of a reward. (He cannot be sure it would cut traffic.)

practice.prompt: Nadia is analysing energy at home. Name one personal-level effect and one global-level connection.
practice.answer: Personal-level effect: the smoke from cooking makes my eyes sting at home. Global connection: burning fuel adds to climate change everywhere.

practice.prompt: A speaker calls the generator 'a filthy, roaring monster'. What does the choice of words tell you about their strength of feeling?
practice.answer: The strong words show a very strong feeling against the generator; the speaker is trying to persuade, not just describe.

practice.prompt: A solution helps older children study at night but adds work for the school cleaner. What kind of analysis has spotted both of these?
practice.answer: Analysing the impacts of a solution on different groups, which looks at who gains and who loses.

vocabulary.meaning: Not in favour of something; seeing reasons not to do it.
The reasons people give for or against an idea.
The good things a solution would bring.
To sort things into groups that belong together.
The reasons why an issue or a problem happens.
A careful judgement reached after weighing the evidence and perspectives.
The results or effects that follow from an issue or a cause.
Information in the form of numbers, counts or measurements.
Facts or information that support an idea or a view.
Things that can be checked and shown to be true.
What you discover after gathering and studying your information.
Changes that make a situation better.
Supporting something; seeing reasons to do it.
The power a person or group has to affect what happens.
The whole job of finding out and analysing an issue.
The set of reasons you give for the solution you choose.
The weaknesses or costs of a solution; what it cannot do.
Things the data does again and again, such as numbers rising in order.
To use words to make someone agree with you or feel something.
The difficulties or issues that people want to solve.
Finding out about an issue in a careful, organised way.
The answers and totals you get after gathering information.
The actions people could take to make an issue better.
Anyone with a real interest in an issue because it affects them or they can affect it.
A way of looking at an issue, shaped by who someone is and where they live.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may dispute.
Saying more than your data proves; something good analysts avoid.
How strongly a person feels about an issue, often shown in the words they choose.
The effects of a solution on different groups of people.

mistakes: Describing only your own perspective and forgetting the others.
Treating a strong opinion as if it were a proven fact.
Naming a cause but forgetting the consequences, or the other way round.
Choosing a solution without weighing the arguments against it.
Forgetting to check who a solution might make worse off.
Over-claiming, by saying more than your data really proves.
Getting stuck at one size, such as only the personal or only the global.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'analysis' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Analysis means breaking an issue into parts to understand it, by asking why it happens, what it leads to, and how different people see it. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)
A perspective is a way of looking at an issue, a point of view shaped by who someone is and where they live.

questions.prompt: Name the three sizes of perspective.
questions.modelAnswer: Personal; local or national; and global.

questions.prompt: True or false: 'Sweets taste nicer than fruit' is a fact.
questions.modelAnswer: False. It is an opinion, because others might disagree; it cannot be checked.

questions.prompt: A ______ is the reason why something happens; a ______ is the result of it happening.
questions.modelAnswer: A cause is the reason why something happens; a consequence is the result.

questions.prompt: Give one signal word that points to a cause, and one that points to a consequence.
questions.modelAnswer: Cause word: any of because, since, due to, the reason is. Consequence word: any of so, therefore, as a result, this leads to.
A stakeholder is anyone with a real interest in an issue, because it affects them or they can affect it.

questions.prompt: When you read a chart, what does the word 'pattern' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: A pattern is something the data does again and again, such as one bar being tallest, or numbers rising or falling in order.

questions.prompt: A justification is the set of ______ you give for the solution you choose.
Name two of the four questions you ask to judge how good a justification is.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: does it give a global reason as well as a local one? does it consider different local perspectives? does it use research? is it honest about strengths and weaknesses?

questions.prompt: Words like 'cruel', 'proud' and 'must' often show the ______ of feeling in a view.
The effects of a solution on different groups of people are called its ______.

selfAssessment.statement: I can recognise that people think differently about an issue, and say why.
I can describe a perspective at three sizes: personal, local or national, and global.
I can tell a fact from an opinion.
I can explain the causes of a local issue and how it affects people.
I can find and describe patterns in data and say what they mean.
I can name the stakeholders in an issue, and who is for it and against it.
I can give arguments for and against ways to solve a local issue.
I can write a justification, giving reasons for the solution I choose.
I can judge how good a justification is, using research and strengths and weaknesses.
I can recognise words that show a strong feeling about an issue.
I can describe how a solution would affect different groups of people.
I can tell what I know for sure from what I can reasonably conclude.
I can find connections between a local issue and a global issue.
